        graph[u - 1].append((v - 1, weight))

    inf = 10**30
    dist = [[inf, inf] for _ in range(n)]
    dist[0][0] = 0
    heap = [(0, 0, 0)]
    while heap:
        cost, u, parity = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if cost != dist[u][parity]:
            continue
        for v, weight in graph[u]:
            next_parity = parity ^ 1
            next_cost = cost + weight
            if next_cost < dist[v][next_parity]:
                dist[v][next_parity] = next_cost
                heapq.heappush(heap, (next_cost, v, next_parity))

    print(-1 if dist[n - 1][0] == inf else dist[n - 1][0])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Common wrong answers

- Running ordinary Dijkstra with one distance per vertex, which loses parity.
- Printing the cheaper of `dist[n][0]` and `dist[n][1]`; only even parity is
  valid.
- Starting at `(1, 1)` instead of `(1, 0)`.
- Counting total edge weight parity instead of the number of roads.
- Marking a state final when it is pushed into the heap rather than skipping
  stale popped entries.

## Tests that matter

- `n = 1` with no roads, whose answer is zero;
- a one-road path to the target, which is unreachable with even parity;
- an odd-hop cheap route and an even-hop more expensive route;
- zero-cost cycles that change parity without changing the cost;
- parallel roads of different costs;
- a long graph with `200000` roads, to test state count and heap behavior.

# Common wrong answers

- Using BFS because the graph is "just shortest path".
- Marking a vertex visited when it is pushed into the heap.
- Forgetting to skip stale heap entries.
- Using 32-bit `int` for distances.
- Applying Dijkstra to negative edges.
- In Discount Route, allowing the discount more than once.

# Stress testing

For small graphs, compare Dijkstra to Floyd-Warshall. For grids, compare to
Floyd-Warshall on the explicit small cell graph or to a slow repeated
relaxation. For Discount Route, build the two-layer graph explicitly and run a
generic Dijkstra to compare against the optimized state implementation.

For Even-Hop Route, build the `2n` parity-state graph explicitly on tiny
inputs and run Floyd-Warshall over those states. This independent oracle catches
the two common modeling errors: starting in odd parity and accepting the
odd-parity destination state. A separate long path with one parity-changing
shortcut checks the `200000`-edge scale.

# What to carry forward

Dijkstra is the default shortest-path algorithm for nonnegative weighted
graphs. The modeling skill is deciding what a state must remember. Once the
state graph has nonnegative edge weights, the same invariant and heap template
apply.


## 10. Get Shorty: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/getshorty>
Local package: [problems/10_get_shorty](problems/10_get_shorty/README.md)

## Restatement

The grid has ordinary open cells, walls, a start, a goal, and lowercase-letter
portal cells.  Walking to an open four-neighbor cell costs `1`.  From a letter
cell, jumping to any cell with that same letter costs `0`.  We need the minimum
cost from `S` to `G`, or `-1` when no route exists.

The grid can contain `10^6` cells.  It is not enough to use ordinary BFS,
because a zero-cost teleport must be processed before a one-cost walk.  It is
also not enough to scan every matching-letter list every time a portal cell is
visited: a grid full of the same letter would become quadratic.

## Model the implicit graph

Use one graph vertex per non-wall grid cell.

```text
walk to a four-neighbor open cell   edge cost 1
same-letter teleport               edge cost 0
```

This is exactly a 0-1 shortest-path problem.  Store the positions of each of
the 26 letters while reading the grid, then use a deque:

```text
cost 0 -> push_front
cost 1 -> push_back
```

## Expanding one portal group once

Suppose the deque first removes a cell labelled `a` at distance `d`.  Every
other `a` cell is reachable from it for cost `0`, so all of them can receive
distance `d` immediately.  There is no reason to scan the complete `a` list
again when another `a` cell is reached later.  Mark the letter as expanded
after this first scan.

The word *first* matters.  In 0-1 BFS, a cell removed from the front has the
smallest currently possible distance.  Therefore the first removed `a` cell
has the minimum distance at which any `a` portal can be reached.

## Walk-through

Consider:

```text
S # a # G
. a . a .
. . . . .
```

Walking from `S` to the left `a` costs `2`:

```text
S -> (1,0) -> left a
```

When that `a` is removed from the deque, expand the `a` group:

```text
left a  -- cost 0 --> right a
```

The right `a` also has distance `2`.  Two ordinary moves reach `G`, so the
answer is `4`.  The longer all-walking detour is never preferable.

## Algorithm

```text
record positions for each letter while reading the grid
dist[cell] = infinity for every cell
dist[S] = 0
push S into a deque
expanded[letter] = false

while deque is not empty:
    remove cell u from the front

    if u has letter x and expanded[x] is false:
        expanded[x] = true
        for every cell v with letter x:
            relax v using cost 0

    for every open four-neighbor v of u:
        relax v using cost 1

print dist[G], or -1 if it is still infinity
```

To relax an edge of cost `w`, update only if:

```text
dist[u] + w < dist[v]
```

Then push `v` to the front for `w = 0`, otherwise to the back.

## Correctness proof

We prove that the algorithm prints the minimum possible cost.

**Lemma 1.** When a portal letter `x` is expanded, the current distance of the
removed `x` cell is the minimum distance of any route from `S` to an `x` cell.

**Proof.** 0-1 BFS removes cells from the deque in nondecreasing finalized
distance order.  The expanded cell is the first removed cell labelled `x`.
If a cheaper route to any `x` cell existed, that cell would have a smaller
distance and would be removed first, a contradiction. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** Expanding each portal letter at most once preserves every
shortest-path distance.

**Proof.** When `x` is expanded at distance `d`, every `x` cell is relaxed to
distance at most `d` by a zero-cost teleport.  By Lemma 1, no `x` cell can
later be reached with a value smaller than `d`.  Thus scanning the same
zero-cost teleport edges later cannot improve any distance. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** Apart from skipped redundant portal scans, the algorithm performs
the same successful relaxations as 0-1 BFS on the implicit graph.

**Proof.** Every walking edge is examined whenever its source cell is removed.
For a portal edge, its whole same-letter group is examined at the first and
minimum-distance source by Lemma 1; Lemma 2 proves later scans are redundant.
Each examined edge is relaxed with its stated cost and sent to the correct end
of the deque. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the minimum travel cost from `S` to `G`, or
`-1` exactly when the goal is unreachable.

**Proof.** By Lemma 3, the algorithm is 0-1 BFS on all useful implicit graph
edges.  The 0-1 BFS invariant therefore gives the shortest distance from `S`
to every reachable cell, including `G`.  If `G` remains at infinity, no
sequence of valid walking or teleport edges reached it, so it is unreachable.
The printed result is consequently correct. $\square$

## Complexity

Each cell has at most four walking edges.  Each portal position appears in one
letter list, and that list is scanned once.  Therefore:

```text
Time:   O(n * m)
Memory: O(n * m)
```

## Implementation notes

- Store letters in 26 lists indexed by `letter - 'a'` or `ord(letter) - ord('a')`.
- Mark a letter expanded before scanning its list.
- A teleport is cost `0`, so its improved endpoints go to the deque front.
- A normal grid step costs `1`, so it goes to the deque back.
- Do not treat `S` and `G` as portal letters; only lowercase characters are
  portal labels.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
    vector<string> grid(n);
    vector<vector<int>> portals(26);
    int start = -1, goal = -1;

    for (int r = 0; r < n; ++r) {
        cin >> grid[r];
        for (int c = 0; c < m; ++c) {
            int id = r * m + c;
            char cell = grid[r][c];
            if (cell == 'S') start = id;
            if (cell == 'G') goal = id;
            if ('a' <= cell && cell <= 'z') {
                portals[cell - 'a'].push_back(id);
            }
        }
    }

    const int INF = 1e9;
    vector<int> dist(n * m, INF);
    vector<char> expanded(26, false);
    deque<int> dq;
    dist[start] = 0;
    dq.push_back(start);
    int dr[4] = {1, -1, 0, 0};
    int dc[4] = {0, 0, 1, -1};

    while (!dq.empty()) {
        int id = dq.front();
        dq.pop_front();
        int r = id / m, c = id % m;
        int current = dist[id];

        char cell = grid[r][c];
        if ('a' <= cell && cell <= 'z' && !expanded[cell - 'a']) {
            expanded[cell - 'a'] = true;
            for (int other : portals[cell - 'a']) {
                if (current < dist[other]) {
                    dist[other] = current;
                    dq.push_front(other);
                }
            }
        }

        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
            int nr = r + dr[k], nc = c + dc[k];
            if (nr < 0 || nr >= n || nc < 0 || nc >= m || grid[nr][nc] == '#') {
                continue;
            }
            int other = nr * m + nc;
            if (current + 1 < dist[other]) {
                dist[other] = current + 1;
                dq.push_back(other);
            }
        }
    }

    cout << (dist[goal] == INF ? -1 : dist[goal]) << '\\n';
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
from collections import deque


def main() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    n, m = map(int, data[:2])
    grid = [row.decode() for row in data[2:2 + n]]
    portals = [[] for _ in range(26)]
    start = goal = -1

    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        for c, cell in enumerate(row):
            cell_id = r * m + c
            if cell == "S":
                start = cell_id
            elif cell == "G":
                goal = cell_id
            elif "a" <= cell <= "z":
                portals[ord(cell) - ord("a")].append(cell_id)

    inf = 10**9
    dist = [inf] * (n * m)
    expanded = [False] * 26
    dist[start] = 0
    dq = deque([start])

    while dq:
        cell_id = dq.popleft()
        r, c = divmod(cell_id, m)
        current = dist[cell_id]
        cell = grid[r][c]

        if "a" <= cell <= "z":
            letter = ord(cell) - ord("a")
            if not expanded[letter]:
                expanded[letter] = True
                for other in portals[letter]:
                    if current < dist[other]:
                        dist[other] = current
                        dq.appendleft(other)

        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < m and grid[nr][nc] != "#":
                other = nr * m + nc
                if current + 1 < dist[other]:
                    dist[other] = current + 1
                    dq.append(other)

    print(-1 if dist[goal] == inf else dist[goal])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Common wrong answers

- Using ordinary BFS, which counts teleports as if they cost one move.
- Putting a zero-cost teleport at the deque back.
- Scanning all cells with letter `a` every time any `a` cell is visited.
- Marking a portal letter used when it is first discovered instead of when it
  is removed at its minimum distance.
- Allowing moves through walls or treating `S` and `G` as lowercase labels.

## Tests that matter

- no portals, which reduces to an ordinary shortest grid path;
- a portal shortcut that is cheaper than the fewest-step walk;
- repeated cells of one letter, to catch repeated full-list scans;
- an unreachable goal;
- a portal first reached by a costly route but later reachable more cheaply;
- a large open grid, which checks linear memory and time.

# Stress testing

On a tiny grid, build the implicit graph literally: from every letter cell,
add a zero-cost edge to every equal-letter cell.  Then run heap Dijkstra and
compare its answer with 0-1 BFS.  This is deliberately slower but independent
of the portal-group optimization.  The local generator uses that oracle on
small random grids and also includes a `1000 x 1000` open grid with known
answer `1998`.

# What to carry forward

0-1 BFS remains linear only when the transition model is also efficient.  A
large group of equivalent zero-cost moves should usually be activated once at
the first finalized distance:

```text
implicit zero-cost group + one-time expansion = linear total work
```

First identify the state and the costs, then account for how often every
generated transition is scanned.


## 11. Coast Length: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/coast>
Local package: [problems/11_coast_length](problems/11_coast_length/README.md)

## Restatement

An undirected, unweighted graph contains several station vertices.  For every
vertex, print the minimum number of edges needed to reach any station.  Print
`-1` when its connected component contains no station.

The graph can have up to `200000` vertices and edges, so running an ordinary
BFS separately from every vertex, or separately from every station, can be
too slow.

## Key idea: start BFS from every station

Imagine adding one virtual source connected to every station by a zero-length
edge.  The desired answer is the shortest distance from that virtual source.
We do not need to build the virtual source: put every station in the BFS queue
initially and assign all of them distance `0`.

Then run the usual BFS.  When a vertex `v` is first discovered from `u`, write

```text
dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
```

Vertices in components without stations are never put in the queue, so their
initial value `-1` remains the correct answer.

## Walk-through

For the chain below, stations are vertices `1` and `5`:

```text
1 -- 2 -- 3 -- 4 -- 5
```

Initial queue and distances:

```text
queue: [1, 5]
dist:  [0, -1, -1, -1, 0]
```

Processing `1` discovers `2`; processing `5` discovers `4`.  Both receive
distance `1`.  Next, either `2` or `4` discovers `3`, which receives distance
`2`.  The answer is therefore:

```text
0 1 2 1 0
```

It does not matter which same-distance vertex is popped first.  BFS always
processes all vertices at distance `d` before any vertex at distance `d + 1`.

## Algorithm

```text
build an adjacency list for the undirected graph
set every dist value to -1

for every station s:
    if dist[s] is -1:          # harmless if a station is listed twice
        dist[s] = 0
        push s into the queue

while the queue is not empty:
    u = pop from the front
    for every neighbor v of u:
        if dist[v] is -1:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
            push v into the queue

print dist[1], dist[2], ..., dist[n]
```

## Correctness proof

We prove that the algorithm prints the required distance for every vertex.

Every station is inserted with distance `0`, so its printed value is correct.
Consider a non-station vertex `v` that is first discovered from `u`.  BFS
processes vertices in nondecreasing distance order.  Thus `u` has the minimum
possible distance to any station among vertices that could first reach `v`.
Appending edge `(u, v)` gives a path of length `dist[u] + 1` from a station to
`v`, so the algorithm assigns a reachable distance to `v`.

Suppose a shorter station-to-`v` path of length `L` existed.  Let `w` be the
vertex directly before `v` on that path.  Because
`L < dist[v] = dist[u] + 1`, we have `L - 1 < dist[u]`.  BFS reaches and
processes `w` before `u`, then discovers `v` with a value at most `L`.  This
contradicts the assignment of the larger value `dist[u] + 1`.  Therefore
`dist[v]` is the minimum distance to any station.

Finally, an unvisited vertex cannot be connected to a station: a path from a
station would make BFS traverse its edges and discover it.  Its value remains
`-1`, which is correct.  Hence all printed values are correct.

## Complexity

Each vertex enters the queue at most once and each undirected edge is examined
twice.  The time complexity is `O(n + m)` and the adjacency list, distances,
and queue use `O(n + m)` memory.

## Reference implementation in C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m, k;
    cin >> n >> m >> k;

    vector<vector<int>> graph(n + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        graph[u].push_back(v);
        graph[v].push_back(u);
    }

    vector<int> dist(n + 1, -1);
    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
        int station;
        cin >> station;
        if (dist[station] == -1) {
            dist[station] = 0;
            q.push(station);
        }
    }

    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        for (int v : graph[u]) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                q.push(v);
            }
        }
    }

    for (int v = 1; v <= n; ++v) {
        cout << dist[v] << (v == n ? '\\n' : ' ');
    }
}
```

## Reference implementation in Python

```python
import sys
from collections import deque


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n, m, k = data[:3]
    index = 3

    graph = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for _ in range(m):
        u, v = data[index], data[index + 1]
        index += 2
        graph[u].append(v)
        graph[v].append(u)

    dist = [-1] * (n + 1)
    q = deque()
    for station in data[index:index + k]:
        if dist[station] == -1:
            dist[station] = 0
            q.append(station)

    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for v in graph[u]:
            if dist[v] == -1:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                q.append(v)

    print(*dist[1:])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Tests worth checking

- One station in a disconnected component: vertices in other components must
  remain `-1`.
- Stations at both ends of a path: the middle vertex uses the closer end.
- Adjacent stations and duplicated station input: every station still has
  distance `0`.
- A long chain with one station at an endpoint: checks both linear time and
  queue behavior.


## 12. All Pairs Shortest Path: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/allpairspath>
Local package: [problems/12_all_pairs_shortest_path](problems/12_all_pairs_shortest_path/README.md)

## Restatement

Every undirected road has a difficulty.  A route is judged by its hardest road,
not by the sum of its road difficulties.  We need the smallest possible value
of that maximum on a route from city `1` to city `n`, or `-1` if no route
exists.  When `n = 1`, the empty route has difficulty `0`.

This wording is a trap: it is not an ordinary shortest path.  Adding a road of
difficulty `4` and one of difficulty `5` gives route difficulty `5`, not `9`.

## Threshold viewpoint

Fix a candidate limit `X`.  Keep only roads with difficulty at most `X`.

```text
There is a route of difficulty at most X
if and only if
1 and n are connected using only roads of difficulty at most X.
```

As `X` increases, roads only get added, so connectivity can only change from
false to true.  Sort all roads by difficulty and add them in that order with a
DSU.  The first difficulty at which cities `1` and `n` share a component is
the answer.

This is related to Kruskal, but we do not need to finish an MST.  Stop as soon
as the two required cities become connected.

## Walk-through

For these roads:

```text
1-3: 3     1-2: 4     3-4: 5     4-5: 5     2-5: 8
```

Process increasing difficulties:

```text
add 1-3 (3): components of 1 and 5 differ
add 1-2 (4): components of 1 and 5 differ
add 3-4 (5): components of 1 and 5 differ
add 4-5 (5): 1 and 5 are now connected
```

The answer is `5`.  The connecting route is `1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5`, whose maximum
edge difficulty is `5`.

## Algorithm

```text
if n is 1:
    print 0
    stop

sort all roads by difficulty
create DSU with one component per city

for each road (u, v, w) in sorted order:
    union(u, v)
    if find(1) equals find(n):
        print w
        stop

print -1
```

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After all roads of difficulty at most `X` have been processed,
the DSU puts two cities in the same component exactly when they are connected
using only roads of difficulty at most `X`.

**Proof.** DSU starts with isolated cities and merges exactly the endpoints of
every processed road.  Thus every DSU merge represents an allowed road path,
and every allowed road is included in the merges.  Its components are exactly
the connected components of the threshold graph. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** When the algorithm first finds cities `1` and `n` connected at
road difficulty `w`, there exists a route from `1` to `n` whose maximum road
difficulty is at most `w`.

**Proof.** All roads processed so far have difficulty at most `w`.  By Lemma
1, DSU connectivity gives a path using only those roads. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** No route from `1` to `n` has maximum road difficulty less than
the first reported value `w`.

**Proof.** Before processing roads of difficulty `w`, the two cities were in
different DSU components.  By Lemma 1, they were disconnected in the graph of
all roads with difficulty below `w`.  Such a route therefore cannot exist.
$\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the required minimum route difficulty, or
`-1` exactly when city `n` is unreachable from city `1`.

**Proof.** Lemmas 2 and 3 show that a reported `w` is feasible and minimal.  If
the scan ends without connecting the cities, Lemma 1 says no input road path
connects them, so `-1` is correct.  The `n = 1` case is correct by the empty
route convention. $\square$

## Complexity

```text
Time:   O(m log m)
Memory: O(n + m)
```

Sorting roads dominates; DSU operations are effectively constant amortized
time.

## Implementation notes

- Use `long long` for road difficulties in C++ even though DSU stores city ids.
- Repeated roads are harmless; DSU ignores a road within an existing component.
- Do not add difficulties along a path.
- Do not return the first road incident to city `n`; check DSU connectivity.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct DSU {
    vector<int> parent, size;
    explicit DSU(int n) : parent(n + 1), size(n + 1, 1) {
        iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);
    }
    int find(int x) {
        return parent[x] == x ? x : parent[x] = find(parent[x]);
    }
    void unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return;
        if (size[a] < size[b]) swap(a, b);
        parent[b] = a;
        size[a] += size[b];
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
    vector<tuple<long long, int, int>> roads;
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        long long w;
        cin >> u >> v >> w;
        roads.emplace_back(w, u, v);
    }
    if (n == 1) {
        cout << 0 << '\\n';
        return 0;
    }
    sort(roads.begin(), roads.end());
    DSU dsu(n);
    for (auto [w, u, v] : roads) {
        dsu.unite(u, v);
        if (dsu.find(1) == dsu.find(n)) {
            cout << w << '\\n';
            return 0;
        }
    }
    cout << -1 << '\\n';
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.parent = list(range(n + 1))
        self.size = [1] * (n + 1)

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a: int, b: int) -> None:
        a = self.find(a)
        b = self.find(b)
        if a == b:
            return
        if self.size[a] < self.size[b]:
            a, b = b, a
        self.parent[b] = a
        self.size[a] += self.size[b]


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    n, m = data[:2]
    roads = sorted(
        (data[i + 2], data[i], data[i + 1])
        for i in range(2, 2 + 3 * m, 3)
    )
    if n == 1:
        print(0)
        return

    dsu = DSU(n)
    for w, u, v in roads:
        dsu.union(u, v)
        if dsu.find(1) == dsu.find(n):
            print(w)
            return
    print(-1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Common wrong answers

- Summing road difficulties and using ordinary shortest-path Dijkstra.
- Building a full MST even after cities `1` and `n` are connected; correct but
  unnecessary.
- Declaring `-1` merely because a low-difficulty prefix is disconnected.
- Forgetting the one-city empty-route case.

## Tests that matter

- city `1` and city `n` disconnected;
- one city and no roads;
- a low-sum route with one very difficult road versus a longer route with a
  lower maximum;
- repeated roads with different difficulties;
- many equal-difficulty roads that connect the endpoints together.

# Stress testing

For small graphs, use a different formulation: minimax Dijkstra.  Let
`dist[v]` be the smallest possible maximum edge on a route to `v`, and relax
an edge of difficulty `w` with:

```text
candidate = max(dist[u], w)
```

Use a heap on that candidate and compare its answer with the DSU threshold
sweep.  The local generator uses this independent oracle for small random
graphs and a direct-answer `200000`-edge scale case.

# What to carry forward

When a route is scored by its worst edge, convert a minimization question into
a connectivity threshold:

```text
"Can I travel using only edges <= X?"
```

Sorting thresholds and DSU are often simpler than forcing an additive shortest
path interpretation.


## 13. Arbitrage: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/arbitrage>
Local package: [problems/13_arbitrage](problems/13_arbitrage/README.md)

## Restatement and observation

We need `a^(b^c) mod P`, where `P = 1000000007` is prime and `a` is nonzero
modulo `P`. Fermat's theorem gives:

```text
a^(P-1) = 1 mod P
```

so only the exponent modulo `P-1` matters. Compute the inner exponent with a
second binary exponentiation:

```text
e = b^c mod (P-1)
answer = a^e mod P
```

For example, `2^(3^2) = 2^9 = 512`.

## Constraints and traps

There can be up to `200000` queries, while `b` and `c` may be enormous. The
outer base is guaranteed not to be divisible by `P`; that contract is vital.

```text
Never form b^c as an ordinary integer.
Reducing the exponent modulo P-1 is valid here only because gcd(a, P) = 1.
The exponent residue may be zero; pow(a, 0, P) correctly returns 1.
Use 64-bit multiplication in C++: products stay below about 10^18.
```

If the base could be zero modulo `P`, the exponent reduction would need a
separate zero/nonzero analysis. This problem deliberately avoids that case.

## Worked trace

Consider `a=2, b=3, c=5`. First compute the inner exponent modulo
`P-1 = 1000000006` by binary exponentiation:

```text
e = 3^5 mod (P-1) = 243
```

Fermat permits replacing the true exponent `3^5` with this residue, so the
second binary power computes `2^243 mod P`. The two powers use the same tool;
only their moduli differ. For a huge `c`, the first call still examines only
the bits of `c`.

## Algorithm

```text
for each query a,b,c:
    exponent = power(b, c, P-1)
    print power(a, exponent, P)
```

Both calls are standard binary exponentiation.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma.** `power(x,y,m)` returns `x^y mod m`.

**Proof.** Binary exponentiation maintains `result * base^remaining` equal to
the original power modulo `m`; each bit either multiplies `result` by the
current power of two or skips it. When remaining becomes zero, the invariant
gives the result. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints `a^(b^c) mod P`.

**Proof.** The first power call returns `e = b^c mod (P-1)` by the lemma.
Because `a` is nonzero modulo prime `P`, Fermat implies exponents differing by
`P-1` give the same residue, so `a^(b^c) = a^e mod P`. The second power call
returns that value by the lemma. $\square$

## Complexity

Each query uses two logarithmic powers:

```text
Time: O(q (log b + log c))
Memory: O(1) besides output
```

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long power(long long base, long long exponent, long long mod) {
    long long result = 1 % mod;
    for (base %= mod; exponent; exponent >>= 1, base = base * base % mod)
        if (exponent & 1) result = result * base % mod;
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int q; cin >> q;
    while (q--) {
        long long a, b, c; cin >> a >> b >> c;
        cout << power(a, power(b, c, MOD - 1), MOD) << '\\n';
    }
}
```

## C++ implementation notes

Use `long long` for the products in binary exponentiation: both operands are
less than `P`, and their product fits in signed 64-bit range. Normalize an
input base with `% MOD` if the statement later allows values outside the usual
range.

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
MOD = 1_000_000_007


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    out = []
    for i in range(data[0]):
        a, b, c = data[1 + 3 * i:4 + 3 * i]
        out.append(str(pow(a, pow(b, c, MOD - 1), MOD)))
    print("\n".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Python implementation notes

Python's three-argument `pow(base, exponent, modulus)` is binary
exponentiation implemented in C. It avoids constructing the enormous integer
`b ** c`; use it for both nested powers.

## Traps and tests

- Reducing the outer exponent by `P-1` requires `a` nonzero modulo `P`.
- Do not compute `b^c` as an ordinary integer.
- Test `b=1`, huge `c`, and base `P-1` with odd/even exponent.

# Stress testing

For tiny bases and exponents, compute `b**c` as an ordinary integer and then
multiply `a` that many times modulo `P`. This independent slow oracle validates
the two modular power calls. The generator also emits 200000 queries with
known answer `2` to exercise input and logarithmic query processing.

# What to carry forward

Under a prime modulus, a nonzero base has exponent period dividing `P-1`.
Nested powers are handled from inside out, reducing each exponent at the
modulus required by the next power.
```


## 14. Knapsack: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/knapsack>
Local package: [problems/14_knapsack](problems/14_knapsack/README.md)

## Restatement and reduction

Let the total of all values be `T`. If one group receives a subset with sum
`s`, the other receives `T - s`, so the split difference is:

```text
|s - (T - s)| = |T - 2s|
```

Thus we need a reachable subset sum as close as possible to `T / 2`. The total
is at most `100000`, so use the section's 0/1 subset-sum DP rather than testing
all `2^n` partitions.

For `1, 6, 11, 5`, `T = 23`. Choosing subset `{11}` gives sums `11` and `12`,
so the answer is `1`.

## Constraints and traps

All values are positive integers and their total `T` is at most `100000`. That
total, rather than the number of input values alone, is the capacity dimension:
an `O(nT)` boolean table is practical, while enumerating `2^n` assignments is
not.

```text
Every occurrence is a separate item, including equal values.
Each occurrence may be assigned to one group exactly once.
There is no requirement that the two sums are equal.
Only a sum s <= T/2 needs final inspection: its complementary sum is T-s.
```

Scanning above `T/2` is redundant. If `s > T/2`, the other group has sum
`T-s < T/2` and represents the same unordered split with the same difference.

## Reachability trace

For values `1, 6, 11, 5`, begin with only sum zero reachable:

```text
after no value:  {0}
after 1:         {0, 1}
after 6:         {0, 1, 6, 7}
after 11:        {0, 1, 6, 7, 11, 12, 17, 18}
after 5:         ... including 11
```

The target half is `23/2 = 11.5`, so the best reachable sum at or below it is
`11`. The resulting difference is `23 - 2*11 = 1`.

When processing `6`, update the boolean array from high sums down to low sums.
For instance, `possible[7]` may use the old `possible[1]`, but that old value
must not already include the current `6`. An upward loop would reach
`possible[12]` through the newly set `possible[6]`, incorrectly using `6`
twice.

## Algorithm

```text
possible[0] = true
for each value x:
    for s from T down to x:
        possible[s] |= possible[s-x]

answer = minimum T - 2*s over reachable s with s <= T/2
```

The loop descends so `possible[s-x]` is still the state before the current
value; each value is used at most once.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After any prefix of values, `possible[s]` is true exactly when a
subset of that prefix sums to `s`.

**Proof.** Initially only the empty subset makes `0`. For new value `x`, a
subset making `s` either omits `x`, or uses it with an earlier subset making
`s-x`. Descending updates implement exactly those two cases without reusing
`x`. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** Every split is represented by a reachable sum `s <= T/2`, and
its difference is `T - 2s`.

**Proof.** Choose the smaller of the two group sums as `s`. The other is
`T-s`, so its difference is `(T-s)-s`. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the minimum possible difference.

**Proof.** Lemma 1 gives exactly every available group sum. Lemma 2 shows the
final scan evaluates every possible split's difference, so its minimum is
optimal. $\square$

## Complexity

```text
Time: O(n * T)
Memory: O(T)
```

where `T` is the total input sum.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n;
    cin >> n;
    vector<int> a(n);
    int total = 0;
    for (int& x : a) {
        cin >> x;
        total += x;
    }
    vector<char> possible(total + 1);
    possible[0] = true;
    for (int x : a) {
        for (int s = total; s >= x; --s) {
            possible[s] = possible[s] || possible[s - x];
        }
    }
    int answer = total;
    for (int s = 0; s <= total / 2; ++s) {
        if (possible[s]) answer = min(answer, total - 2 * s);
    }
    cout << answer << '\\n';
}
```

## C++ implementation notes

`vector<char>` is a compact boolean table and avoids the unusual proxy behavior
of `vector<bool>`. The table has indices `0` through `total`, inclusive. The
descending loop condition is `s >= x`, so `s-x` is always a valid index.

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    values = data[1:]
    total = sum(values)
    possible = bytearray(total + 1)
    possible[0] = 1
    for value in values:
        for current in range(total, value - 1, -1):
            if possible[current - value]:
                possible[current] = 1
    print(min(total - 2 * s for s in range(total // 2 + 1) if possible[s]))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Python implementation notes

Use `bytearray(total + 1)` for a compact mutable reachability table;
`possible[0]` must start true. In Python, `range(total, value - 1, -1)` is the
descending 0/1 update. Only sums through `T/2` need inspection after the DP,
although updating through `T` keeps the transition simple.

## Common wrong answers

- An upward loop accidentally permits a value multiple times.
- Requiring an exactly half-total subset instead of accepting the closest one.
- Deduplicating equal input values even though they are separate items.

## Tests that matter

- one value;
- an odd total;
- an exactly balanced input;
- repeated values;
- total sum `100000`.

# Stress testing

For at most 18 values, enumerate every bitmask and minimize `abs(T - 2*s)`.
This independent brute-force oracle checks the DP on random small cases. The
local generator separately uses one hundred values of `1000` for the
`100000`-sum scale case.

# What to carry forward

Partition questions often become subset-sum DP after expressing both group
sums in terms of one selected subset. Derive the algebra first, then choose the
capacity state and its loop direction.


## 15. Clock Pictures: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/clockpictures>
Local package: [problems/15_clock_pictures](problems/15_clock_pictures/README.md)

## Restatement and traps

For every prefix length `L`, count all substring occurrences of that prefix,
including overlaps. With `n <= 200000`, comparing every prefix at every start
is quadratic. The whole string itself occurs once, and a singleton prefix can
occur many times.

## Observation and trace

Let `pi[i]` be the longest proper prefix ending at position `i`. Every prefix
ending at `i` contributes one occurrence to length `pi[i]`; that occurrence
also belongs to every border of that prefix. Count direct `pi` values, then
propagate counts from long lengths to their failure link:

```text
for x in pi: count[x]++
for length from n-1 down to 1:
    count[pi[length-1]] += count[length]
answer[length] = count[length] + 1
```

The final `+1` counts the prefix occurrence beginning at position zero. Here is
the complete small trace for `ababa`:

```text
index i:       0 1 2 3 4
character:     a b a b a
pi[i]:         0 0 1 2 3
```

Directly incrementing the nonzero `pi` values gives:

```text
length L:      1 2 3 4 5
direct count:  1 1 1 0 0
```

Now propagate in decreasing length. Length `3` passes its one occurrence to
its failure link `pi[2]=1`; the resulting relevant counts are:

```text
after L=3:     count[1]=2, count[2]=1, count[3]=1
```

Lengths `2` and `1` only pass counts to the zero-length sentinel. Adding the
initial occurrence to every positive length gives `3 2 2 1 1`. In particular,
the occurrence of `aba` also contributes to its border `a`; that is exactly
what the failure-link propagation preserves.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma.** After propagation, `count[L]` is the number of non-initial
occurrences of the prefix of length `L`.

**Proof.** Every occurrence ending at a position first contributes to its
longest proper prefix match. Its failure-link chain lists exactly all shorter
prefixes that also end there. Processing links from longer to shorter passes
each occurrence to every such border once. $\square$

**Theorem.** `count[L]+1` is the total occurrence count of prefix length `L`.

**Proof.** The lemma counts all occurrences ending after the initial prefix;
the unmatched initial occurrence contributes the one added explicitly. $\square$

## Complexity

The prefix function and failure-link propagation are both `O(n)` time and use
`O(n)` memory.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);string s;cin>>s;int n=s.size();vector<int>pi(n),cnt(n+1);for(int i=1;i<n;i++){int j=pi[i-1];while(j&&s[i]!=s[j])j=pi[j-1];if(s[i]==s[j])j++;pi[i]=j;}for(int x:pi)cnt[x]++;for(int i=n-1;i>0;i--)cnt[pi[i-1]]+=cnt[i];for(int i=1;i<=n;i++)cout<<cnt[i]+1<<(i==n?'\n':' ');}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
 s=sys.stdin.buffer.readline().strip();n=len(s);pi=[0]*n;cnt=[0]*(n+1)
 for i in range(1,n):
  j=pi[i-1]
  while j and s[i]!=s[j]:j=pi[j-1]
  if s[i]==s[j]:j+=1
  pi[i]=j
 for x in pi:cnt[x]+=1
 for i in range(n-1,0,-1):cnt[pi[i-1]]+=cnt[i]
 print(*(cnt[i]+1 for i in range(1,n+1)))
if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

## Tests and stress testing

Test `a`, `aaaa`, and a string with no repeated prefix. For tiny strings, the
oracle directly compares every prefix against every legal substring start;
this is independent of prefix links. The scale case is `200000` copies of
`a`, whose answers are `n,n-1,...,1`, exposing quadratic matching.


## 16. String Matching: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/stringmatching>
Local package: [problems/16_string_matching](problems/16_string_matching/README.md)

## Restatement

For every input word, find the shortest nonempty prefix shared by exactly one
input occurrence. Equal words are still separate occurrences, so no prefix can
distinguish one copy from another. A word that is a prefix of a longer word may
also have no answer.

This is the blind trie exercise for the section: the task asks for a property
of all prefixes of each word, not merely a count for one supplied prefix.

## Constraints and traps

There are up to `200,000` words and the same bound on total characters. Testing
every prefix against every word is quadratic. The answer is an input-order
answer, so duplicate words need repeated `-1` lines rather than being merged.

Do not mistake "the word ends here" for "the prefix is unique." For `do` and
`dog`, the prefix `do` is a prefix of both input words even though only one
word ends at that trie node.

## Observations and trace

In a trie, store `pass[node]`: the number of input words whose path visits the
node. During insertion, increment it after every character. Then a prefix is
unique exactly when the node reached by that prefix has `pass == 1`.

Insert the sample's `cat`, `car`, `dog`, `do`, `cat`. The node for `ca` has
`pass=3` because it serves both copies of `cat` and `car`. The node for `car`
has `pass=1`, so `car` needs length three. The node for `do` has `pass=2`, and
there is no later node for the shorter word `do`, so its answer is `-1`.

## Algorithm

```text
make a trie whose nodes store child links and pass counts
for every word:
    walk/create its character path
    increment pass at each reached node

for every word in input order:
    walk its trie path from the root
    print the first position whose node has pass = 1
    print -1 if no such position occurs
```

## Correctness proof

**Lemma.** For every trie node representing prefix `p`, `pass[node]` equals
the number of input words beginning with `p`.

**Proof.** A word visits exactly the nodes for its nonempty prefixes during
insertion. The algorithm increments this node once for that word and never for
a word that does not have the prefix. Summing over all input occurrences gives
the stated count. $\square$

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the required shortest unique-prefix length
for every word.

**Proof.** By the lemma, a scanned prefix is unique exactly when its node has
`pass=1`. The second traversal checks prefixes in increasing length order, so
the first such node is the shortest valid prefix. If none is found, every
nonempty prefix is shared by at least two occurrences and `-1` is correct.
$\square$

## Complexity

Let `L` be the total input length.

```text
Time:   O(L)
Memory: O(L)
```

## C++ implementation notes

An `array<int,26>` gives fixed lowercase transitions. A node index of zero is
the root; newly allocated children receive positive indices. Increment only
the destination node's `pass` count, because the empty prefix is not allowed.

## Python implementation notes

A list of dictionaries keeps the implementation direct. Use byte input for
large files if desired; the reference decodes after splitting because input is
restricted to lowercase ASCII.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
struct Node { array<int,26> next{}; int pass = 0; };
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; if (!(cin >> n)) return 0; vector<string> words(n); vector<Node> trie(1);
    for (string &word : words) { cin >> word; int node = 0; for (char ch : word) { int c=ch-'a'; if (!trie[node].next[c]) { trie[node].next[c]=trie.size(); trie.push_back(Node{}); } node=trie[node].next[c]; ++trie[node].pass; } }
    for (const string &word : words) { int node=0, answer=-1; for (int i=0;i<(int)word.size();++i) { node=trie[node].next[word[i]-'a']; if (trie[node].pass==1) { answer=i+1; break; } } cout << answer << '\n'; }
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def main() -> None:
    words = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    if not words: return
    n = int(words[0]); words = [word.decode() for word in words[1:n + 1]]
    children = [{}]; passed = [0]
    for word in words:
        node = 0
        for char in word:
            if char not in children[node]:
                children[node][char] = len(children); children.append({}); passed.append(0)
            node = children[node][char]; passed[node] += 1
    output = []
    for word in words:
        node = 0; answer = -1
        for length, char in enumerate(word, 1):
            node = children[node][char]
            if passed[node] == 1: answer = length; break
        output.append(str(answer))
    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(output) + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__": main()
```

## Common wrong answers

```text
Counting only words ending at a node instead of every word passing through it.
Deduplicating equal strings before answering.
Returning a prefix for do when dog is also present.
Using the root count as an empty-prefix answer.
Scanning all words for every candidate prefix.
```

## Tests that matter

```text
Identical words: every copy must print -1.
A word that is a prefix of another word.
Words sharing a long prefix before branching.
A one-word input: answer is 1 for a nonempty word.
200,000 identical one-letter words: checks linear memory and output.
```

# What to carry forward

Advanced algorithms become manageable when you state the invariant first, then code only the operations needed to preserve it.

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Trie Prefix Count

Every node is one prefix and `count[node]` is the number of inserted words that
visit it. Insert `apple, ape, bat`: the node for `ap` has count two, while a
missing query edge returns zero immediately. Insert every word character by
character, incrementing the root and child after each move; walk each query and
return the endpoint count. The invariant follows by induction over inserted
words: exactly the words having a prefix pass through that node. Work is linear
in total inserted and queried characters, with one node per distinct prefix.
Use fixed 26-child arrays in C++ for lowercase input, dictionaries in Python for
clarity. Test duplicate words, one word that is a prefix of another, absent
queries, and a one-character query.

## B. Palindrome Queries

The local bounds permit exact two-pointer checking. Convert inclusive 1-based
`l,r` to zero-based positions, then compare outward characters while `l<r`.
For `abacaba`, `[2,4]` is `bac` and fails at `b,c`; `[3,5]` is `aca` and passes.
A substring equals its reverse iff every mirrored pair is equal, which proves
the test. A query costs `O(r-l+1)`, with `O(1)` extra memory; this is not the
right technique for very large query limits. C++ can use `substr` plus reverse
under the local contract, Python can use `s[l-1:r] == s[l-1:r][::-1]`. Test
singletons, full string, even and odd lengths, and a mismatch at the center's
outside pair.

## C. Distinct Substrings

The full listing uses a suffix automaton. After reading a prefix, `last` is the
state for that entire prefix; each state has maximum represented length `len`
and a suffix link to the largest proper suffix state. State v represents new
substring lengths `len[link[v]]+1..len[v]`, so its contribution is
`len[v]-len[link[v]]`. Summing non-root contributions counts every nonempty
distinct substring once. A clone copies transitions when the existing target
cannot have the required `len[p]+1`; redirecting suffix transitions restores
the state invariant. For `ababa`, the answer is nine. There are at most
`2*n-1` states and `O(n)` transitions for a fixed alphabet (the map-based local
listing is `O(n log alphabet)`). Test `a`, `aaa`, all distinct characters, and
an alternating string. Python dictionaries make the same construction viable.

## 17. Max Flow: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/maxflow>
Local package: [problems/17_max_flow](problems/17_max_flow/README.md)

## Restatement and reduction target

Each project has a possibly negative profit. A directed rule `a b` means that
selecting project `a` requires selecting project `b`. Choose any feasible set
of projects, including the empty set, with maximum total profit. There can be
up to `200` projects and `1,000` rules, so enumerating all subsets is impossible.

This is a maximum-closure problem. A cut represents which projects are chosen:
put a project on the source side exactly when it is selected. We will construct
the network so that a finite cut is exactly a feasible choice, and its capacity
is the profit lost by that choice.

## Network construction and trace

Let `P` be the sum of all positive project profits. Build a source `s` and sink
`t` around the project vertices:

```text
profit w > 0:  add s -> project with capacity w
profit w < 0:  add project -> t with capacity -w
rule a requires b: add a -> b with capacity INF
```

Choose `INF = P + 1`. No optimum cut can afford an `INF` edge because cutting
every positive source edge costs at most `P`. Therefore a finite minimum cut
never puts `a` on the source side while `b` is on the sink side: it obeys every
requirement.

For profits `[9,-5,7,-3]` with rules `1->2`, `3->4`, and `3->2`, selecting all
projects earns `9-5+7-3=8`. In the corresponding cut, no positive source edge
is cut and the two negative project-to-sink edges cost `5+3=8`. Since
`P=16`, `P-cut=8`. Selecting only project 1 and its prerequisite 2 has profit
4 and cuts source edge for project 3 (cost 7) plus project 2's sink edge
(cost 5), again `16-12=4`.

## Algorithm

```text
P = sum of positive profits
INF = P + 1
build the stated flow network
min_cut = maximum_flow(s, t)
print P - min_cut
```

The max-flow/min-cut theorem supplies the minimum cut value. Use `long long`
for `P`, `INF`, capacities, and the result.

## Correctness proof

Consider any feasible selected set `S` and place exactly its projects with the
source. No prerequisite edge crosses from source to sink because feasibility
ensures every requirement of a selected project is also selected. The cut
crosses `s -> v` for every unselected positive project, and `v -> t` for every
selected negative project. Its capacity is therefore

```text
sum(positive profits of unselected projects)
+ sum(absolute negative profits of selected projects)
= P - profit(S).
```

Conversely, a minimum cut cannot cross an `INF` edge: cutting all source edges
has cost `P < INF`. Thus its source-side projects satisfy every prerequisite,
so they form a feasible set, and the same equality shows their profit is
`P - cut_capacity`. Minimizing cut capacity therefore maximizes feasible profit.
By max-flow/min-cut, the computed maximum flow is that minimum capacity, so
the algorithm prints the optimal profit. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

The network has `n+2` vertices and `n+m` forward edges. It uses `O(n+m)` memory.
With arbitrary integral capacities, Dinic has worst-case `O(V^2 E)` time;
the deliberately moderate local bound (`n <= 200`, `m <= 1000`) makes this
implementation appropriate in both supplied languages. For substantially
larger arbitrary-capacity maximum-closure networks, use a flow implementation
and limits whose performance guarantee has been analyzed for that setting.
`INF` must be strictly larger than the total positive profit, not a small magic
constant. Test all-negative projects (answer zero), a profitable project whose
requirements make it unprofitable, independent profitable projects, and rules
forming a cycle.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Dinic {
    struct Edge {
        int to, reverse;
        long long capacity;
    };

    vector<vector<Edge>> graph;
    vector<int> level, next_edge;

    explicit Dinic(int n) : graph(n), level(n), next_edge(n) {}

    void add_edge(int from, int to, long long capacity) {
        Edge forward{to, (int)graph[to].size(), capacity};
        Edge backward{from, (int)graph[from].size(), 0};
        graph[from].push_back(forward);
        graph[to].push_back(backward);
    }

    bool build_levels(int source, int sink) {
        fill(level.begin(), level.end(), -1);
        queue<int> queue;
        level[source] = 0;
        queue.push(source);
        while (!queue.empty()) {
            int vertex = queue.front();
            queue.pop();
            for (const Edge& edge : graph[vertex]) {
                if (edge.capacity > 0 && level[edge.to] == -1) {
                    level[edge.to] = level[vertex] + 1;
                    queue.push(edge.to);
                }
            }
        }
        return level[sink] != -1;
    }

    long long send_flow(int vertex, int sink, long long pushed) {
        if (vertex == sink) return pushed;
        for (int& edge_index = next_edge[vertex];
             edge_index < (int)graph[vertex].size(); edge_index++) {
            Edge& edge = graph[vertex][edge_index];
            if (edge.capacity == 0 || level[edge.to] != level[vertex] + 1) continue;
            long long flow = send_flow(edge.to, sink, min(pushed, edge.capacity));
            if (flow == 0) continue;
            edge.capacity -= flow;
            graph[edge.to][edge.reverse].capacity += flow;
            return flow;
        }
        return 0;
    }

    long long max_flow(int source, int sink) {
        long long total = 0;
        const long long INF = numeric_limits<long long>::max() / 4;
        while (build_levels(source, sink)) {
            fill(next_edge.begin(), next_edge.end(), 0);
            while (long long pushed = send_flow(source, sink, INF)) total += pushed;
        }
        return total;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    if (!(cin >> n >> m)) return 0;
    vector<long long> profit(n);
    long long positive_total = 0;
    for (long long& value : profit) {
        cin >> value;
        if (value > 0) positive_total += value;
    }

    int source = n;
    int sink = n + 1;
    Dinic flow(n + 2);
    long long inf = positive_total + 1;
    for (int project = 0; project < n; project++) {
        if (profit[project] > 0) flow.add_edge(source, project, profit[project]);
        if (profit[project] < 0) flow.add_edge(project, sink, -profit[project]);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        int project, prerequisite;
        cin >> project >> prerequisite;
        flow.add_edge(project - 1, prerequisite - 1, inf);
    }

    cout << positive_total - flow.max_flow(source, sink) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
from collections import deque


class Dinic:
    def __init__(self, size: int) -> None:
        self.graph: list[list[list[int]]] = [[] for _ in range(size)]
        self.level = [-1] * size
        self.next_edge = [0] * size

    def add_edge(self, start: int, end: int, capacity: int) -> None:
        self.graph[start].append([end, len(self.graph[end]), capacity])
        self.graph[end].append([start, len(self.graph[start]) - 1, 0])

    def build_levels(self, source: int, sink: int) -> bool:
        self.level = [-1] * len(self.graph)
        self.level[source] = 0
        queue = deque([source])
        while queue:
            vertex = queue.popleft()
            for target, _, capacity in self.graph[vertex]:
                if capacity > 0 and self.level[target] == -1:
                    self.level[target] = self.level[vertex] + 1
                    queue.append(target)
        return self.level[sink] != -1

    def send_flow(self, vertex: int, sink: int, pushed: int) -> int:
        if vertex == sink:
            return pushed
        while self.next_edge[vertex] < len(self.graph[vertex]):
            edge = self.graph[vertex][self.next_edge[vertex]]
            target, reverse, capacity = edge
            if capacity > 0 and self.level[target] == self.level[vertex] + 1:
                flow = self.send_flow(target, sink, min(pushed, capacity))
                if flow:
                    edge[2] -= flow
                    self.graph[target][reverse][2] += flow
                    return flow
            self.next_edge[vertex] += 1
        return 0

    def max_flow(self, source: int, sink: int) -> int:
        total = 0
        while self.build_levels(source, sink):
            self.next_edge = [0] * len(self.graph)
            while pushed := self.send_flow(source, sink, 10**30):
                total += pushed
        return total


def main() -> None:
    tokens = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not tokens:
        return
    n, m = tokens[0], tokens[1]
    profit = tokens[2 : 2 + n]
    pointer = 2 + n
    positive_total = sum(value for value in profit if value > 0)
    source, sink = n, n + 1
    flow = Dinic(n + 2)
    inf = positive_total + 1
    for project, value in enumerate(profit):
        if value > 0:
            flow.add_edge(source, project, value)
        elif value < 0:
            flow.add_edge(project, sink, -value)
    for _ in range(m):
        project, prerequisite = tokens[pointer] - 1, tokens[pointer + 1] - 1
        pointer += 2
        flow.add_edge(project, prerequisite, inf)
    print(positive_total - flow.max_flow(source, sink))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.setrecursionlimit(300_000)
    main()
```

# Complete upsolve notes

## A. Max Flow

Each added edge stores a forward residual capacity and a reverse edge initially
of capacity zero. Pushing f along an edge subtracts f forward and adds f to the
reverse edge; this preserves capacities and allows rerouting. Dinic BFS assigns
shortest residual levels, then DFS only follows edges from level d to d+1 until
the level graph is blocking. If BFS cannot reach sink, no residual augmenting
path exists, hence max-flow/min-cut proves the accumulated flow maximum.

On the sample, send two units through 1-2-4 and two through 1-3-4; the edge
2-3 capacity one is not required, and the value is four. Pseudocode:

```text
while BFS(source) reaches sink:
    reset current-edge pointers
    while DFS(source, infinity) pushes f > 0: answer += f
```

The standard Dinic bound is `O(V^2 E)` for arbitrary integral capacities; it is
comfortably adequate for the local exercises. Use `long long` for capacities and
flow, and update the reverse edge at the same moment as the forward edge. Test
no path, parallel edges, a bottleneck, and a case requiring a reverse residual
edge to reroute earlier flow.

## B. Bipartite Matching

`match_right[v]` is the left vertex currently owning right vertex v, or -1. A
DFS from an unmatched left vertex explores right neighbors. An unused right
matches immediately; an occupied right can be taken only if its owner finds an
alternative recursively. This chain is an augmenting path, so each successful
root DFS increases the matching by one. If every unmatched left root fails,
there is no augmenting path and the matching is maximum.

For edges L1-R1,R2 and L2-R1, first match L1-R1; the L2 search reroutes L1 to
R2 and then takes R1, yielding two pairs. Reset visited-right for each root.
This Kuhn implementation costs `O(L*E)` in the worst case and is appropriate
for the local small matching limits; use Hopcroft-Karp for larger instances.
Test no edges, duplicate-looking choices, a reroute case, and unequal part
sizes.

## C. Min Cut Reachable Side

Run the same max-flow routine, then BFS from source using only final residual
edges of positive capacity. Let S be reached vertices. If an original forward
edge left S with residual capacity, BFS would cross it; therefore all such
edges are saturated. Their capacity equals the maximum flow, so S is the source
side of a minimum cut. On the max-flow sample, inspect the final residual graph
rather than the original graph before printing vertices. The extra BFS costs
`O(V+E)` after Dinic. Test source-only reachability, all vertices reachable
when flow is zero, and parallel crossing edges.

## 18. Min Cut: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/mincut>
Local package: [problems/18_min_cut](problems/18_min_cut/README.md)

## Restatement and reduction target

Each project has a possibly negative profit. A directed rule `a b` means that
selecting project `a` requires selecting project `b`. Choose any feasible set
of projects, including the empty set, with maximum total profit. There can be
up to `200` projects and `1,000` rules, so enumerating all subsets is impossible.

This is a maximum-closure problem. A cut represents which projects are chosen:
put a project on the source side exactly when it is selected. We will construct
the network so that a finite cut is exactly a feasible choice, and its capacity
is the profit lost by that choice.

## Network construction and trace

Let `P` be the sum of all positive project profits. Build a source `s` and sink
`t` around the project vertices:

```text
profit w > 0:  add s -> project with capacity w
profit w < 0:  add project -> t with capacity -w
rule a requires b: add a -> b with capacity INF
```

Choose `INF = P + 1`. No optimum cut can afford an `INF` edge because cutting
every positive source edge costs at most `P`. Therefore a finite minimum cut
never puts `a` on the source side while `b` is on the sink side: it obeys every
requirement.

For profits `[9,-5,7,-3]` with rules `1->2`, `3->4`, and `3->2`, selecting all
projects earns `9-5+7-3=8`. In the corresponding cut, no positive source edge
is cut and the two negative project-to-sink edges cost `5+3=8`. Since
`P=16`, `P-cut=8`. Selecting only project 1 and its prerequisite 2 has profit
4 and cuts source edge for project 3 (cost 7) plus project 2's sink edge
(cost 5), again `16-12=4`.

## Algorithm

```text
P = sum of positive profits
INF = P + 1
build the stated flow network
min_cut = maximum_flow(s, t)
print P - min_cut
```

The max-flow/min-cut theorem supplies the minimum cut value. Use `long long`
for `P`, `INF`, capacities, and the result.

## Correctness proof

Consider any feasible selected set `S` and place exactly its projects with the
source. No prerequisite edge crosses from source to sink because feasibility
ensures every requirement of a selected project is also selected. The cut
crosses `s -> v` for every unselected positive project, and `v -> t` for every
selected negative project. Its capacity is therefore

```text
sum(positive profits of unselected projects)
+ sum(absolute negative profits of selected projects)
= P - profit(S).
```

Conversely, a minimum cut cannot cross an `INF` edge: cutting all source edges
has cost `P < INF`. Thus its source-side projects satisfy every prerequisite,
so they form a feasible set, and the same equality shows their profit is
`P - cut_capacity`. Minimizing cut capacity therefore maximizes feasible profit.
By max-flow/min-cut, the computed maximum flow is that minimum capacity, so
the algorithm prints the optimal profit. QED.

## Complexity, implementation notes, and tests

The network has `n+2` vertices and `n+m` forward edges. It uses `O(n+m)` memory.
With arbitrary integral capacities, Dinic has worst-case `O(V^2 E)` time;
the deliberately moderate local bound (`n <= 200`, `m <= 1000`) makes this
implementation appropriate in both supplied languages. For substantially
larger arbitrary-capacity maximum-closure networks, use a flow implementation
and limits whose performance guarantee has been analyzed for that setting.
`INF` must be strictly larger than the total positive profit, not a small magic
constant. Test all-negative projects (answer zero), a profitable project whose
requirements make it unprofitable, independent profitable projects, and rules
forming a cycle.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct Dinic {
    struct Edge {
        int to, reverse;
        long long capacity;
    };

    vector<vector<Edge>> graph;
    vector<int> level, next_edge;

    explicit Dinic(int n) : graph(n), level(n), next_edge(n) {}

    void add_edge(int from, int to, long long capacity) {
        Edge forward{to, (int)graph[to].size(), capacity};
        Edge backward{from, (int)graph[from].size(), 0};
        graph[from].push_back(forward);
        graph[to].push_back(backward);
    }

    bool build_levels(int source, int sink) {
        fill(level.begin(), level.end(), -1);
        queue<int> queue;
        level[source] = 0;
        queue.push(source);
        while (!queue.empty()) {
            int vertex = queue.front();
            queue.pop();
            for (const Edge& edge : graph[vertex]) {
                if (edge.capacity > 0 && level[edge.to] == -1) {
                    level[edge.to] = level[vertex] + 1;
                    queue.push(edge.to);
                }
            }
        }
        return level[sink] != -1;
    }

    long long send_flow(int vertex, int sink, long long pushed) {
        if (vertex == sink) return pushed;
        for (int& edge_index = next_edge[vertex];
             edge_index < (int)graph[vertex].size(); edge_index++) {
            Edge& edge = graph[vertex][edge_index];
            if (edge.capacity == 0 || level[edge.to] != level[vertex] + 1) continue;
            long long flow = send_flow(edge.to, sink, min(pushed, edge.capacity));
            if (flow == 0) continue;
            edge.capacity -= flow;
            graph[edge.to][edge.reverse].capacity += flow;
            return flow;
        }
        return 0;
    }

    long long max_flow(int source, int sink) {
        long long total = 0;
        const long long INF = numeric_limits<long long>::max() / 4;
        while (build_levels(source, sink)) {
            fill(next_edge.begin(), next_edge.end(), 0);
            while (long long pushed = send_flow(source, sink, INF)) total += pushed;
        }
        return total;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, m;
    if (!(cin >> n >> m)) return 0;
    vector<long long> profit(n);
    long long positive_total = 0;
    for (long long& value : profit) {
        cin >> value;
        if (value > 0) positive_total += value;
    }

    int source = n;
    int sink = n + 1;
    Dinic flow(n + 2);
    long long inf = positive_total + 1;
    for (int project = 0; project < n; project++) {
        if (profit[project] > 0) flow.add_edge(source, project, profit[project]);
        if (profit[project] < 0) flow.add_edge(project, sink, -profit[project]);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        int project, prerequisite;
        cin >> project >> prerequisite;
        flow.add_edge(project - 1, prerequisite - 1, inf);
    }

    cout << positive_total - flow.max_flow(source, sink) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## 19. Distributing Ballot Boxes: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/distributingballotboxes>
Local package: [problems/19_distributing_ballot_boxes](problems/19_distributing_ballot_boxes/README.md)

## Restatement and predicate

Machines run in parallel; machine i produces `floor(minutes / time[i])` items
by a proposed deadline. The question "can we make at least goal items by x?"
is monotone: if it is true at x, it stays true at every later minute.

## Bounds, trace, and algorithm

Zero minutes is infeasible because the goal is positive. `min(time) * goal` is
feasible because the fastest machine can work alone; the local bounds keep it
inside signed 64-bit range. With times 2 and 3, seven items need nine minutes:
at eight minutes production is `4+2=6`, while at nine it is `4+3=7`.

```text
lo = 0; hi = fastest_time * goal
while lo < hi:
    mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2
    if sum(mid / time[i]) >= goal: hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
print lo
```

## Correctness proof

For any x, each machine's production is exactly `floor(x/time[i])`, so the
predicate computes total production correctly. Increasing x cannot decrease
any term, hence feasibility is monotone. The binary-search invariant keeps lo
infeasible (unless it is the answer boundary) and hi feasible; each iteration
retains the first feasible value in the interval. When they meet, that value is
the minimum feasible deadline, which is the requested answer.

## Complexity and implementation notes

Each predicate is O(n), so the solution is `O(n log(min_time*goal))` time and
O(n) memory for the input. In C++, use `long long` and stop summing once total
reaches goal to avoid unnecessary growth. Python integers are safe, but the
same early break is useful. Test one machine, goal one, equal machine times,
and a case near the 64-bit bound. The random tests use minute-by-minute brute
force only on small instances plus a 200000-machine scale case.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int test_count;
    cin >> test_count;

    while (test_count--) {
        int n;
        long long goal;
        cin >> n >> goal;

        vector<long long> time(n);
        for (long long& x : time) {
            cin >> x;
        }

        long long lo = 0;
        long long hi = *min_element(time.begin(), time.end()) * goal;

        while (lo < hi) {
            long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            long long made = 0;

            for (long long machine_time : time) {
                made += mid / machine_time;
                if (made >= goal) break;
            }

            if (made >= goal) {
                hi = mid;
            } else {
                lo = mid + 1;
            }
        }

        cout << lo << '\n';
    }
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def minimum_deadline(time: list[int], goal: int) -> int:
    lo = 0
    hi = min(time) * goal

    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        made = 0

        for machine_time in time:
            made += mid // machine_time
            if made >= goal:
                break

        if made >= goal:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1

    return lo


data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
i = 1
out = []

for _ in range(data[0]):
    n = data[i]
    goal = data[i + 1]
    i += 2
    time = data[i:i + n]
    i += n
    out.append(str(minimum_deadline(time, goal)))

sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))
```


## 20. Catering: local companion

External Kattis task: <https://open.kattis.com/problems/catering>
Local package: [problems/20_catering](problems/20_catering/README.md)

## State expansion

The free-edge coupon is part of the route history. Reaching the same vertex
before and after using it are different situations, so use states `(vertex,used)`
where `used` is zero or one. From `(v,used)`, an edge of weight `w` gives
`(to,used)` at cost `w`; when `used=0`, it also gives `(to,1)` at cost zero.

All expanded-edge costs are nonnegative, so run Dijkstra from `(1,0)`. The
answer is the smaller distance to `(n,0)` and `(n,1)`.

## Correctness proof

Every legal original route maps to exactly one expanded path by marking whether
its coupon has already been used. Its expanded cost equals its paid cost.
Conversely, every expanded path uses at most one zero-cost coupon transition,
so it maps to a legal route of the same cost. Dijkstra returns shortest paths
in this nonnegative expanded graph; therefore the reported minimum is optimal.

## Complexity and tests

The expanded graph has `2n` states and at most `4m` directed transitions, so
Dijkstra costs `O((n+m) log n)` time and `O(n+m)` memory. Test one edge (answer
zero), a route where the most expensive edge is not on the ordinary shortest
path, and a long chain. The tiny oracle uses repeated edge relaxation on both
coupon layers; the scale case is a 200000-vertex chain.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n,m;if(!(cin>>n>>m))return 0;vector<vector<pair<int,long long>>>g(n);while(m--){int a,b;long long w;cin>>a>>b>>w;--a;--b;g[a].push_back({b,w});g[b].push_back({a,w});}const long long I=4e18;vector<vector<long long>>d(2,vector<long long>(n,I));priority_queue<array<long long,3>,vector<array<long long,3>>,greater<array<long long,3>>>q;d[0][0]=0;q.push({0,0,0});while(!q.empty()){auto[x,u,v]=q.top();q.pop();if(x!=d[u][v])continue;for(auto[to,w]:g[v]){if(x+w<d[u][to])d[u][to]=x+w,q.push({x+w,u,to});if(!u&&x<d[1][to])d[1][to]=x,q.push({x,1,to});}}cout<<min(d[0][n-1],d[1][n-1])<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys,heapq
def main():
 d=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
 if not d:return
 n,m=d[:2];g=[[] for _ in range(n)];i=2
 for _ in range(m):
  a,b,w=d[i]-1,d[i+1]-1,d[i+2];i+=3;g[a].append((b,w));g[b].append((a,w))
 inf=10**30;dist=[[inf]*n for _ in range(2)];dist[0][0]=0;pq=[(0,0,0)]
 while pq:
  cost,used,v=heapq.heappop(pq)
  if cost!=dist[used][v]:continue
  for to,w in g[v]:
   if cost+w<dist[used][to]:dist[used][to]=cost+w;heapq.heappush(pq,(cost+w,used,to))
   if not used and cost<dist[1][to]:dist[1][to]=cost;heapq.heappush(pq,(cost,1,to))
 print(min(dist[0][-1],dist[1][-1]))
if __name__=='__main__':main()
